claim: Contact-transition stability is distinct from coupled stability after contact: even when the in-contact equilibrium is asymptotically stable, an impedance-controlled robot may rebound and lose unilateral contact before impact energy is absorbed. For the paper's linearized SISO, stiffness-dominated environment and position-based impedance architecture, the target damping ratio is the dominant design variable; a large environment-to-target stiffness ratio, corresponding to high commanded compliance against a stiff surface, requires strongly overdamped target behavior. In the ideal delay-free model the derived transition bound depends on damping and stiffness ratios but not target natural frequency, whereas force-measurement and computation delay raises the required damping and makes target frequency important. Manutec-r3 experiments support these model-based bounds within the tested ranges, but do not establish general stability for nonlinear, multi-contact, highly uncertain, or time-varying impedance systems.
claim_locator: Abstract; Section 1 Introduction; Section 2 Mathematical Model, Eqs. 1-2; Section 3 Position Based Impedance Control, Eqs. 3-11 and Figs. 1-2; Section 4 Contact Stability Criteria, Eqs. 12-17 and Figs. 3-4; Sections 4.1, 5.2, and 5.3 on time-domain, delay, friction, and input/output criteria, Eqs. 18-28 and Fig. 5; Section 5 Experimental Tests, Figs. 6-7; Section 6 Conclusion.
epistemic_status: Full-text primary analytical and experimental study. Transition criteria are theorem- or derivation-supported only for the stated linearized SISO and input/output models; agreement with hardware bounds is author-reported and was not independently reproduced.
problem_and_setting: A contact task comprises free-space gross motion, constrained compliant motion, and transition phases between them. Earlier analyses often asked whether an already-contacting robot-environment interconnection remains stable, but not whether first impact establishes continuous unilateral contact without bouncing. The paper studies an industrial position-controlled robot commanded to a nominal position behind a stiff obstacle and asks which target impedance parameters prevent loss of contact while absorbing impact energy.
method_or_mechanism: The robot is linearized in Cartesian space around a nominal trajectory, with Coriolis and centrifugal effects neglected at low contact velocity and gravity assumed ideally compensated. The passive environment is modeled locally as a linear mass-damper-stiffness relation, then simplified to dominant stiffness. Position-based impedance control retains the industrial robot's inner position servo and closes an outer force-sensing loop that modifies the commanded position to realize a diagonal target mass-damper-stiffness impedance. Transition stability is defined pragmatically by positive endpoint penetration or nonnegative contact force after first impact. For an ideal position servo and SISO contact direction, the resulting second-order penetration dynamics are solved in time domain. Necessary and sufficient loss-of-contact conditions are obtained by locating the critical phase-plane point where penetration returns to zero, although controller synthesis requires solving transcendental equations; a conservative estimate yields a minimum target damping ratio. A frequency-domain alternative requires the coupled impedance to be positive real, and an infinity-norm small-gain criterion provides a simpler sufficient, conservative bound applicable to continuous or discrete systems and able to include delay and uncertainty weights. A retarded differential model explicitly represents force-information delay; its characteristic quasipolynomial must have all roots in the open left half-plane.
content_summary: The paper sharpens impedance-control stability analysis by separating equilibrium stability from impact-transition stability. Its ideal target model can have an asymptotically stable in-contact equilibrium while the physical unilateral constraint is violated transiently by rebound. Stable transition therefore requires penetration to remain positive, equivalently contact force to remain nonnegative in the selected compliance direction. In the ideal second-order SISO model, positive nominal acceleration at contact, greater target damping, and higher target frequency support continuous contact; for constant-velocity impact, the minimum damping is determined from the derived critical-point equations. The reported key result is that the delay-free stability boundary depends on target damping ratio and the environment-to-target stiffness ratio, not on target frequency. High compliance against a stiff environment produces a large stiffness ratio and requires significant overdamping. Coulomb friction enters through the position-loop sensitivity and is argued to be negligible for a stiff industrial position servo and directionally helpful because it resists loss of contact. Delay has the opposite effect: delayed force information significantly increases required damping, makes natural frequency consequential, and is identified experimentally as a crucial cause of contact loss. The infinity-norm criterion is more conservative than the time-domain bound but easier to compute and incorporate model uncertainty. Experiments on a Manutec-r3 used an 8 ms computation cycle and maximum 8 ms force-sensing/computation delay, a goal 8 mm beyond a 60000 N/m environment, target stiffnesses from 250 to 8000 N/m, target frequencies from 0.5 to 8 Hz, and masses selected from 0.1 to 200 kg. Reported transition boundaries agreed closely with the delayed second-order model at 6-8 Hz and relatively low stiffness ratios; at 0.5-1 Hz, greater damping was needed. The 8 Hz setting approached the position-loop bandwidth and was discouraged for practical use. The conservative infinity-norm rule always prescribed more damping. The authors report lower minimum damping than earlier criteria, allowing faster response and smaller impact-force overshoot.
synthesis_role: Transition-stability card that converts the early continuous-impedance idea into explicit design rules for establishing contact on industrial position-controlled robots. It identifies damping, relative stiffness, impact trajectory, bandwidth, and sensing delay as separate contributors and provides both less-conservative time-domain and robust-but-conservative input/output criteria.
development_link: Earlier impedance control showed that one continuous controller could span free and constrained motion without mode switching, but empirical stability did not explain when impact would cause repeated separation. This paper adds a unilateral-contact criterion and derives damping boundaries for position-based impedance control on geared industrial robots, where prior direct-drive mass-ratio rules were not applicable. It advances practical synthesis by including force delay and a conservative uncertainty-compatible norm test, while leaving later work to handle nonlinear robot and contact dynamics, uncertain or changing environments, simultaneous contacts, friction beyond a disturbance argument, and online variation or learning of impedance parameters.

evidence.statement: The paper distinguishes coupled stability during maintained contact from transition stability, defined as establishing continuous contact after first impact without multiple impacts.
Stable transition is represented by positive penetration or nonnegative contact force for all times after first contact, so an asymptotically stable equilibrium alone is insufficient.

The analysis uses a Cartesian-linearized robot, a passive linear environment reduced mainly to stiffness, and diagonal SISO target impedance dynamics along each constrained compliance-frame direction.

For the ideal SISO second-order model, necessary and sufficient transition conditions are defined by the critical phase-plane point where penetration reaches zero; computing the exact boundary requires transcendental equations.
In the ideal delay-free case, the minimum damping boundary depends on target damping ratio and environment-to-target stiffness ratio but is independent of target natural frequency.
evidence.support_scope: Section 4.1 conclusion following the critical-point estimate.

evidence.statement: High commanded compliance against a stiff environment requires a significantly overdamped target impedance to preserve contact.
Positive nominal acceleration at impact, increasing damping ratio, and increasing target frequency are reported to support stable transition in the considered trajectory model.
Coulomb friction is argued to have little effect within a stiff position servo's bandwidth and to resist contact separation, making the ideal frictionless result conservative for this architecture.
evidence.support_class: analytical approximation and directional inference by authors

evidence.statement: Force-information delay is represented by a retarded differential equation whose stationary solution is asymptotically stable only when all characteristic quasipolynomial roots have negative real parts.
Delay substantially raises required damping and makes target frequency important; higher frequency or lower target mass can help address delay, subject to position-loop bandwidth.

The positive-real condition is necessary along each SISO constrained direction, while the infinity-norm criterion is sufficient and conservative but applies to continuous and discrete delayed systems and can incorporate uncertainty weights.
Manutec-r3 experiments used 8 ms control and force-delay bounds, 60000 N/m environmental stiffness, an 8 mm nominal penetration, target stiffness 250-8000 N/m, and target frequency 0.5-8 Hz.

The delayed second-order model reportedly predicted transition bounds accurately at 6-8 Hz and relatively low stiffness ratios; low-frequency cases required more damping, and the norm bound was consistently more conservative.
The authors report that their minimum damping bounds are lower than prior recommendations, yielding faster response and smaller transition-force overshoot.

evidence_kind: Linearized Cartesian modeling, exact and approximate SISO time-domain transition derivation, retarded-system characteristic-root analysis, positive-real and infinity-norm input/output criteria, and author-reported industrial-robot contact experiments; no nonlinear multi-contact theorem or broad statistical validation.
boundary_conditions: The central analytic conditions are SISO results applied separately along constrained compliance-frame directions; cross-axis coupling is suppressed by diagonal-dominance and spatial-rounding assumptions.
Robot dynamics are linearized near a nominal trajectory; Coriolis and centrifugal terms are neglected for low contact velocity and gravity is assumed ideally compensated.
The environment is passive and linear mass-damper-stiffness in the general model, then primarily approximated as pure stiffness for transition analysis.

The contact is unilateral and represented by endpoint penetration into one surface; adhesion, frictional stick-slip, plastic impact, deformation, and multiple simultaneous contacts are not modeled fully.

The position-based architecture assumes a stable, robust, stiff industrial position servo and an outer force loop; conclusions need not apply unchanged to torque-controlled or admittance-controlled robots.
The ideal exact time-domain solution assumes an ideal position servo and specified initial conditions at first contact; discontinuous trajectory derivatives require segment-wise treatment.

The geometric error-versus-nominal-penetration criterion is not globally valid; the paper argues it is convenient for stiff industrial servos and relatively rigid environments whose impedances exceed the target impedance.
The delay-free frequency independence applies only to the ideal second-order model; with delay, target frequency materially affects stability.

The retarded-system statement requires all quasipolynomial roots to have negative real parts; the practical boundary is obtained numerically through an equivalent nondelayed representation referenced by the paper.
The positive-real frequency-domain inequality is necessary under Hurwitz target and environment polynomials; the infinity-norm rule is only sufficient and intentionally conservative.
The claim that Coulomb friction is negligible and stabilizing relies on small position-loop sensitivity and motion-resisting friction; other friction regimes may not satisfy this approximation.
Higher target frequency is limited by the inner position-control bandwidth, reported heuristically as about half that bandwidth; the tested 8 Hz case was already near the practical limit.
Experimental validation is limited to one Manutec-r3 system, one environment stiffness, one nominal penetration, and the enumerated target parameter ranges.

The experiments estimate stability boundaries from repeated parameter-set transitions but the text does not report statistical confidence intervals, trial counts per set, or raw outcome distributions.
Uncertainty weighting is described as possible within the norm criterion but is not shown as a comprehensive experimental robust-uncertainty study.
The paper analyzes fixed target parameters during a transition; it does not certify online variable or learned impedance.
assumptions: The supplied full text faithfully represents the paper despite OCR omissions in several displayed equations.

Symbols are interpreted from prose and legible equations: K=Ke/Kt is the environment-to-target stiffness ratio, the target damping ratio is the main design variable, and target frequency is set by stiffness and mass.
The phrase necessary and sufficient is retained only for the paper's specified ideal or retarded SISO formulations, not for the full industrial robot.
Experimental statements are treated as author-reported validation rather than independent replication.
The link to variable and learning impedance is a synthesis of the fixed-parameter boundary problem and is not a claim that this paper implements adaptation.

reported: An impedance-controlled robot may have a stable in-contact equilibrium yet bounce and lose contact during the initial transition.
Previously proposed high target inertia and damping rules can make free-motion and loss-of-contact response sluggish and can produce high forces or long transition times.
High compliance against a stiff environment requires substantial overdamping in the analyzed system.
Force sensing and computation delay significantly increases the damping required for transition stability and is identified as a crucial influence on contact loss.
At low target frequencies of 0.5-1 Hz, the hardware required higher damping than the simpler bound predicted.
A target frequency of 8 Hz approached the inner position-control bandwidth and was considered unsuitable for practical use.
The infinity-norm criterion overestimates the required damping relative to less-conservative methods.
inferred: Applying the scalar damping bound independently by axis may miss destabilizing Cartesian coupling, configuration dependence, or noncollocated structural modes.
Online gain variation or learning could cross the derived fixed-parameter boundary or inject energy, so separate stability supervision would be required.
Unknown environment stiffness changes the stiffness ratio directly and can invalidate a damping choice made from an inaccurate contact model.
The pure-stiffness environment approximation may underrepresent dissipative, inertial, hysteretic, or nonlinear contact effects.
A higher target frequency can mitigate delay only until bandwidth, noise, discretization, or unmodeled dynamics reverse the benefit.
The experimental match on one industrial robot does not establish robustness to arbitrary impact velocities, geometries, multiple contacts, active environments, or large model errors.
